explanation.text: The June 2022 HTTP standard classifies POST as an unsafe method, not safe. Multiple sources confirm safe methods are GET, HEAD, OPTIONS (and TRACE, QUERY in some listings), while POST is consistently listed under unsafe methods alongside PUT, DELETE.
The assertion that POST counts as a safe method contradicts the cited HTTP standard definitions which explicitly exclude POST from safe methods.
Official HTTP specifications and glossaries from June 2022 define safe methods as read-only operations; POST is classified as unsafe because it modifies server state through data submission.

excerpts.text: An HTTP method is **safe** if it doesn't alter the state of the server.

Several common HTTP methods are safe: [`GET`](/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Methods/GET), [`HEAD`](/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Methods/HEAD), or [`OPTIONS`](/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Methods/OPTIONS). All safe methods are also [idempotent](/en-US/docs/Glossary/Idempotent), but not all idempotent methods are safe.

* Definition of [safe](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9110.html#safe.methods "External link (opens in new tab)") in the HTTP specification.
* Description of common safe methods: [`GET`](/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Methods/GET), [`HEAD`](/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Methods/HEAD), [`OPTIONS`](/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Methods/OPTIONS)
* Description of common unsafe methods: [`PUT`](/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Methods/PUT), [`DELETE`](/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Methods/DELETE), [`POST`](/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Methods/POST)

excerpts.text: The biggest addition to HTTP in sixteen years arrived in June 2026, when the IETF published [RFC 10008](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc10008/) and gave the web a new method called QUERY. It is the first new standard HTTP verb since PATCH landed in 2010, and it was authored by Julian Reschke, James Snell and Mike Bishop after a conversation that Asbjørn Ulsberg reopened at the 2019 HTTP Workshop.
A POST can carry a rich body, but it is neither safe nor idempotent, so caches skip it, clients cannot safely retry it, and intermediaries must assume it changes state.
